messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 45
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Journalist
  trauma_type: Captivity
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic Pain (Neck): Neck pain, Tactile (Touch): Physical touch, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, False Alarms: I often react as if I am in danger even when nothing is actually wrong, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Memory Replay: My memories of the frightening event are like a film that plays over and over., Uncontrolled Access: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Daniel Weber is a 45-year-old married American journalist who came to treatment after years of trying to manage on his own what he still calls “that time I was held.” While reporting abroad, he was taken captive and kept for a period in a small room by armed men who controlled when he could sleep, eat, move, and speak. What remains most vivid to him is not an orderly story but a set of sensory moments that feel as if they are still happening. He remembers being forced down onto a chair and restrained, the sharp strain through his neck as his head was yanked back and held there during questioning. He remembers the closeness of other bodies in the room, hands gripping his shoulders and jaw without warning, and the stale smell of liquor on one captor’s breath when the man leaned over him to talk. In his recollection, these details are not distant. The scene returns “like a film,” as Daniel puts it, complete and moving, and when it comes back he feels the same terror he felt then, as if his body has not understood that the captivity ended.

In the months after his release, Daniel tried to return to work and to the life he had with his wife. He told himself that as a journalist he should be able to keep going, file copy, tolerate pressure, and stay composed. Instead he found that memories forced themselves into his mind without his wanting them. He could be sitting at his desk editing an interview transcript and suddenly the image of the chair, the hands, the room would start replaying with a terrible immediacy. When this happened, he did not experience it as remembering in the ordinary sense; it felt more like being seized by the event again. What frightened him most was how quickly terror returned. He was certain, in those moments, that he was about to be overpowered, even when he was in his own office or at home.

Over time he became increasingly watchful in ways that shaped his days. In the newsroom, where phones rang, doors slammed, and conversations rose unexpectedly behind him, Daniel stayed on edge. A dropped camera bag or a burst of laughter from across the room could make him jolt before he had time to think. He often reacted as if danger were present even when nothing was wrong, scanning the room and tracking movement before he could settle himself. He began choosing a seat with a clear view of the door in editorial meetings and avoiding crowded press events when he could. He knew colleagues noticed that he startled easily at loud or sudden sounds, but he could not stop monitoring the environment for what might happen next.

His specific triggers are woven into ordinary moments. Neck pain is one of the strongest. If he wakes with stiffness after sleeping badly, or if long hours bent over a laptop bring on an ache, he is abruptly pulled back to the position in which his head was forced and held. The pain does not merely remind him; it seems to open the whole scene. Physical touch can do the same. His wife placing a hand unexpectedly on the back of his neck, a colleague brushing past him in a hallway, even a routine pat on the shoulder can produce an immediate surge of alarm before he recognizes where he is. He has tried to explain to his wife that it is not about her, but the recoil has nonetheless changed the texture of their marriage. The smell of alcohol is especially potent. On assignment receptions, in restaurants, or passing someone on the street who has been drinking, he catches the odor and is instantly back in the room with a captor leaning close enough for Daniel to smell liquor on his breath.

These experiences have accumulated into a narrower life. Daniel now structures his work to reduce the likelihood of being caught off guard, preferring phone interviews over in-person events and leaving noisy gatherings early. At home he is tense around sudden sounds and remains superalert even in safe settings, listening for shifts in the house and reacting before he has assessed what he heard. He has come to believe that his mind can turn on him without warning, that memory can break through at any moment and trap him in the worst part of his life.

He finally sought help after a recent incident at work when a coworker came up behind him to get his attention just as neck pain had been building from a long day at the computer. Daniel spun around in panic, heart racing, disoriented and ashamed, then had to leave the office after the familiar film of the captivity began replaying in full. What he fears most is that he will remain at the mercy of these moments, always one sound, one touch, or one smell away from terror. What he hopes for, cautiously, is not to erase what happened but to be able to live beside it without feeling dragged back into captivity each time his body or surroundings echo the past.
